Mr. Chairman, the right hon. gentleman has anticipated a phase of this discussion upon which I was about to embark. The whole theory of reports being made to council by the responsible minister is that they may be discussed in council. I pointed out many weeks ago, when it had been stated that it was a one man government, that hon. members had overlooked the fact that the president of the council had to call upon ministers to state why a certain action should be taken. They made their reports and upon those reports tfhe action was taken. Discussion took place freely and sometimes lasted many hours with respect to what action should be taken. In some instances the clerk, anticipating that action would be taken along the lines of the report, prepared a draft order. This has been done by successive clerks. I shall not review what has been said over and over again by the Secretary of State. These reports are not acted upon in their entirety. They are sent back to the ministers to be revised or rewritten, or changes are made therein counselled by the ministers. The order in council is then prepared. If time is pressing, interlineations are sometimes written into the body of the draft order in council itself and initialled by the president of the council and sent out in due course to the clerk of the council so that the approval of the executive may be obtained. If, after discussion, a conclusion is arrived at and the responsibility for the preparation of the document finally rests with the prime minister, his colleagues may say to him: "We have settled the principle, you will settle the order; if you will settle it and make the interlineations as we have
agreed upon them, we will sign on the distinct understanding that the principle has been settled." That happened not only under this government, but under many governments.

It is the first time I ever heard that.

If they had not received these moneys and paid them into the general banking account, the Canadian wheat board would have had to assume a much greater adverse bank balance than it has at the present time; that is the justification from the point of view of the wheat board legislation for the repayment to the wheat pools of these three sums.
If an examination were made of the situation I think it would be found that if the sum provided for in the original order in council had been paid out, there would have been authorized to be paid out the sum of $1,402,461.36 without statutory authority. I arrive at that figure in this manner. I have added the two amounts that appear in the auditor's report, the sum of $890,658.44 for coarse grains, and the sum of $862,487.57 for expenses, making a total .of $1,753,146.01, which had nothing to do with wheat except to the extent that the wheat balance would have been greater than it now is had it not been for the fact that the amounts that were owing to rye producers, flax producers and barley producers went into the general banking account; therefore it is proper to deduct that $350,684.65, leaving the sum which I mentioned, $1,402,461.36. The order in council, if it had been acted upon, would have resulted in that expenditure without authorization.
Now, what was the purpose and what was the advantage of passing an order in council if the government was going to get an auditor's report first?
To authorize the payment.

Why pass it in the expeditious manner that was adopted? Why not get the auditor's report and make a thorough examination first to verify the amounts, and also to verify whether the transaction that was being approved was one relating exclusively to wheat or otherwise? Why was that not done before the order in council was drafted? That is a question that might well be asked, and I say that this discussion has served a useful purpose in indicating the care that should be taken before we legislate by order in council. It is well that all the facts should be disclosed before the committee, and that this legislation should be passed in the form and in the manner which is suggested.
Surely my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition cannot be serious when he suggests that there is no authority in this house to pass this legislation.
I did not say that.

Why, of course, there is authority, and if it should be necessary to add a clause to the effect that so far as this particular transaction is concerned, section 7, paragraph f, should to that extent be repealed, it would be a simple thing to do. I suggest that the passing of the statute following this resolution would operate as a repeal pro tanto of the section we have been discussing. I would much rather see legislation of this sort passed in the manner in which we are passing it than see it passed in the manner disclosed by the discussions of yesterday and to-day. To that extent the discussion that occurred yesterday and again to-day has, in my opinion, served a very useful purpose.

I am a little surprised
at the turn the discussion has taken. As I understand it, an agreement was reached between the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, and the government prior to the election. I think my understanding is similar to that of the people of western Canada. We believe that the money mentioned in this order in council was to do four things: First, it was to equalize all pool wheat payments at sixty cents per bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not equalize; that would be quite impossible.

To settle on that basis. Next, it was to bring the spreads into proper relationship so that the producers who delivered would not be penalized on account of lower grades. I am particularly interested in the third item, to adjust all coarse grain payments.
A lot of people had that idea.

That is the general
idea throughout western Canada. Four, to provide for the operating costs of the provincial pools for the 1930 crop. I have given this order in council a very careful study indeed. Paragraph (b) was quoted a few moments ago by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson). The phraseology is this:
The Canadian wheat board will pay to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, the sum of eight millions, two hundred and sixty-two thousand, four hundred and fifteen dollars and thirty-seven cents ($8,262,415.37),-
Then occurs a comma. When the minister was reading this particular paragraph this afternoon I asked him to say whether the

Wheat Board
word was "and" or "the" following the word "producers" in the paragraph as it continues:
-being the sum total of balances due to the primary producers,-
Not the wheat producers only but the primary producers.
-and expenses and other charges in connection with the holding and handling of the wheat.
I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) shaking his head, but I rose in my place to point out that this is not only my impression but that of thousands of people throughout western Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have good reason to
know that, because they have written to me to tell me that is what they were promised.

That is a factor which
must be considered at this time by this parliament. The producers of western Canada believe that the basis which I have outlined briefly was the basis of this particular agreement. Why do they believe that? Because they believe that the wheat and the other grains, which were their grains, were used throughout these difficult years to bring about a certain measure of stability. In connection with oats, where the auditors report a loss, there is a general opinion that they were more or less retained at the request, with the consent, or upon the advice of the then governments concerned, dominion and provincial, because of the peculiar drought, feed and seed conditions which were prevalent that year and the following years in western Canada. I urge the government to take these matters into consideration.
In other countries the farmers have been bonused very heavily. Fortunately for the Canadian people the farmers of this dominion had built up an organization which gave to agriculture something in the way of stability. It was a low stability, if you will, but nevertheless the institutions were there and the government of this country did not bonus the producers as was done in France, in the Argentine republic, in Australia and in the United States to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars. As I said the other day, western Canada contains 55,000,000 of the
73,000,000 acres of cultivated land in the dominion. This vast area is in bad condition because of economic and natural causes over which the people had no control. I urge the government to read this order in council as I believe it is read by the producers of western Canada, and, when the bill is brought down, to see to it that the money allotted is sufficient to take care of all the payments the producers expect with regard to grain,
even if the administration costs of the pool are deducted. This would increase the amount further by some 8500,000, but I submit that that amount would not be a gift; it would not be a compassionate allowance; it would be payment for services rendered by these classes of producers to the people and the government of Canada during the difficult years through which we have just passed.

I think I nodded my
head when the hon. member mentioned the figure of $500,000. The amount will be about $1,250,000.
Yes. Total amount.

If the government would
only show a little Christian charity towards the head of the late government (Mr. Bennett) in connection with this matter it would enhance the opinion which the ratepayers of this country have toward this parliament. I think the head of the late government made one of the most outstanding contributions to the welfare of Canada. I have made a deep study of this question for over twenty years. A great protectionist paper in Toronto, the Evening Telegram, spent from $15,000 to $20,000 in 1922 to investigate the grain industry in the prairie provinces, the greatest imperial industry in this country. I know of no man who knows more about this grain industry than does the head of the late government. He is fully conversant with the functions of the producers, the traders, the handlers, the carriers, the millers and every one else engaged in this industry. There were some thirteen inquiries made by this parliament and provincial legislatures into this industry from 1897 to 1914.
This matter was dealt with late in June and in the early part of July of last year, when the Prime Minister of that day brought down an important measure which would have improved for all time the condition of the grain growers of western Canada. It is important for us to know just where the money in the resolution will go, and what I am concerned about in connection with this resolution is to see that the fund goes into the pockets of the men who grow the grain. Too long have these pools and grain exchanges been handled, not by practical farmers but by men who had not the interests of the grain growers primarily at heart but were party first farmers. When I look around this building and see lobbying lawyers and old officials of the grain exchanges, the very men who are responsible for the lot of the poor grain grower, I can sympathize with the late
Wheat Board

Prime Minister, who did more to place the industry on a sound basis than did any other man in Canada. He saved not only the grain industry but the country from bankruptcy during the worst years of the depression. He did not create these conditions; they were created years before he came into office-by whom? By the Liberal party, by the Liberal premier of Saskatchewan and other prairie Liberals, who spoke liere to-day, and by other Liberal premiers of the three prairie provinces. Their doctrine was that this greatest of imperial industries was a continental industry, and they insisted on the quack remedy of free trade. That was their cure-all for the ills of the prairies, with the result that this industry has been one of the worst exploited in Canada.
Years ago, Mr. Chairman, when you first came into this house, there was an effort on the part of the Conservative party to have coal, iron and steel and grain protected and supported by means of bonuses, subsidies and subventions. Protection has always been the best friend of the western grower and that policy has been extended by the founders and authors of protection, the Conseravtive party. But the Liberal party has advocated free trade, and we find that the western wheat growers have eaten the sour grapes of free trade; it is no wonder their teeth are on edge. The western wheat grower has allowed his leaders to delude him into thinking that wheat is a continental industry, but I submit that it is the greatest of imperial industries, for the markets of the British empire mean more to the grain growers of Canada than to any other class of producers in the country. The greatest enemy the western wheat grower has had has been the free trade policy of hon. gentlemen opposite and of the Liberal premiers of the three prairie provinces. They are the people who got the grain grower into his present state. On the other hand, the leader of the opposition, during his term of office as Prime Minister, did more for the western wheat grower than any other man in Canada has done. I think, therefore, he received a raw deal from the very men who should have appreciated what he had done for them, the men actually growing grain on the prairies.
I would not have taken part in this debate but for the fact that two members of the cabinet yesterday met a deputation from the municipalities. I said the other day that fifty per cent of the workers in central Canada were engaged in industrial pursuits; the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Crerar) increased that percentage when he estimated it at fifty-three per cent.
I must ask the hon. member to confine himself to the resolution. There is nothing about protection or free trade in the resolution.

Is that correct, Mr. Chairman, but we are naturally anxious to know where the money is going to come from. The minister has given an explanation with which I am not at all satisfied. He was a free trader, and now he is for grain protection. It is true that this is only a resolution; we are told to wait until the bill comes down. Well, if this is the only industry that is to receive financial assistance from parliament, how much longer will the central provinces stand for the payment of these moneys when the industrial workers are refused consideration along similar lines? This resolution is based on the doctrine of protection, not free trade.
I believe in protection for all grain growers, but I would point out that some of the grain growers do not belong to the pool, nor do they wish to belong to the pool. I know that if I were out there I would not belong to a pool. No doubt this will benefit some of the grain growers, but there are others who will not get anything out of it. The whole system is wrong and in my opinion we should have a national policy for the handling of grain. We should provide protection for the men growing the grain so that the profits will not accrue to the grain exchanges. I look upon the grain exchanges as the aristocracy in this industry.
When will the payments be made? No one knows. Like a returning officer in an election, these men will probably be paid six months or a year after payment is due. And where do the farmers of Ontario come in? The minister said that there were four pools in Saskatchewan and Manitoba dealing with coarse grains but that there was none in Alberta. I do not know how long the finances of the country will stand this sort of paternalism. These stabilization funds are protection and are a burden and paid for by the industrial workers of Ontario, and they should have some protection as well as the grain grower. I am not opposed to the resolution; I believe that, properly administered, the legislation forecast therein would have a good effect, but I am opposed to a hand-out of $111,000,000 without any investigation. One thing the former Prime Minister did; in connection with this order in council that has been so much discussed, was that he insisted on putting some commercial restriction and some brake on the granting of these funds, instead of allowing himself to be dictated to by the grain exchange. What are these

Wheat Board
grain exchange people doing around the parliament buildings in the last few days? One newspaper gives their names. I could name a good many of them, although I am not going to do so, men who are trying to use their influence to bolster up these funds, not only the grants under this resolution, but something else that is coming down, $111,000,000 that has been handed out already, and more asked for.
A few years ago the three prairie provinces could get along with a grant or a cash subsidy under the British North America Act; they were able to maintain themselves without any subventions; they carried on their financial affairs the same as did other provinces in this confederation. I believe in the principle of confederation, the old Cornish battlecry of "Each for all and all for each." Ontario industrialists and farmers are just as much interested in the prairies as are other people, because every man, woman and child in every province except the Yukon are interested in the grain industry, as the Prime Minister said last July, in the success of these measures, and it was due very largely to him that proper commercial restrictions were applied in connection with the order in council. I think he is to be commended by the business men of the country for having prevented, as in the opinion of every good citizen he did prevent, province-wide bankruptcy in this great industry.
The people of Ontario and Quebec are becoming much alarmed at the obligations entailed by such resolutions as the one presented to-day, for a sum for $6,500,000 in respect of coarse grains and $350,000 for some other growers. Then these debentures are added on; wait till you see the expense bill. You probably will not find the expenses contained in the bill; they will be in the auditor general's report or a return to an order of the house.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Who produced the wheat, who sold it, who bought it, and who is now going to pay for it? Why should the farmers of Ontario enter into that transaction in any place at all? It is not a hand-out.

That is not a question. That is a speech. I can only say that there is going to be a show-down in this house on social credit. So far as the merchants of Ontario and Quebec are concerned there are not going to be any more hand-outs along the lines proposed by the hon. member's party. The industrial workers have certain rights and privileges in this house. We want some
return for our money. I believe the time is not far distant when the two old provinces will insist on having a survey made. Surveys have been made all over; let us have a survey of Ontario and Quebec and find out what our real place in confederation is, instead of being a hewer of wood and a drawer of water for the rest of confederation.

What I am concerned about is the amount involved that is to be paid over, and how soon it will be paid. On page 1464 of Hansard the 'hon. minister is reported as having said last night that his reason for being anxious to get along with this legislation was that seed grain has to be put out in western Canada within the next few weeks, and that if this 86,000,000 goes out to the farmers there, it will be a great help. The contract is over $8,000,000.
Between six and seven millions.
The order in council, the agreement with the pool, was over $8,000,000, and $350,000 for coarse grains. Can the minister give us the amount that will go forward on the wheat?

The amount covered
by the order in council was SS,262,000. That included almost a million dollars that was supposed to be for expenses; that would have gone to the pools to cover expenses, and included almost a million dollars for coarse grain; or, to be more exact, between eight and nine hundred thousand dollars for coarse grains. The amount that is to be paid out in this present bill is $6,509,000 for wheat, and $350,000 in round figures, for flax, rye and barley. These amounts will be paid out just as soon as we get this bill through the house and regulations set up upon which the payments are to be made.

The speech of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) raised two or three questions that I should like to have answered now. When were the coarse grains sold, and who is to disburse the cheques? The hon. minister says now, when they get the regulations ready The contract is between the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, and the wheat board, and the wheat board, not the government, were the people who made the purchase of the wheat. I want to know who is going to make the payments.

The bill makes provision, at least the intention of the bill is to make provision, for the payment of the moneys
Wheal Board

from the wheat board to the wheat pool organizations, through the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, which is the central organization at Winnipeg of the three pools. The procedure followed by the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, in the past has been to pass over whatever moneys are available to the three provincial pools, and the three provincial pools have made the distribution. The bill will provide that regulations for the payment, after the money reaches the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, are to be agreed to by the governor general in council. These regulations will be submitted by the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, to the government before the payments are actually made.
I probably was not strictly correct in saying, in reply to the hon. member for the Battlefords, that $350,000 will be paid out to the producers by the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited. That amount of money will be turned over to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, and it is expected that at least a part of it, if not all of it, will be paid to the primary producers. It is really their money, and we are not presuming to say to them what they have to do with it, but the intention is that that is where it should go. Probably I was more nearly correct last evening than I was a moment ago when I said that the amount was over $6,000,000. It would be about $6,500,000 that we are sure will go to the producers; the other amount we are hoping will go to the producers. The amount that goes out for the coarse grains, shall I give the figures again? I gave them last night; they are already on Hansard.

No. The speech of the hon. member for Selkirk indicates that he has a much greater knowledge of this transaction than I have. What I desired to know was, when there was the realization on the coarse grains, because I think in view of what he has said I can offer an explanation about some meanings that were difficult to see until a moment ago.
In order to give full information on that I would have to read the auditor's report, pages 24, 25, 26; there are about ten pages or so of it.
It is not necessary to do that. Perhaps the hon. minister can answer shortly in this way: Were the coarse grains disposed of prior to January 1, 1935? That would be broad enough to cover the matter.

I think so, broadly
speaking. There is a table which sets that out. Probably I had better get the table.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It varies as between the different grains.
I know, but I am asking about them all.

Of wheat,-this is the carry-over in 1933-the total carry-over was
76,375,000	bushels. That was about sixty per cent of the amount taken in in 1930. Then, of oats, 1,265,000 bushels. That is about twenty-four per cent of the amount of oats that was originally taken in, and still held in 1933. Of barley there were 676,000 bushels, or about 10| per cent of what was taken in during 1930. Of flax there were only 7,000 bushels left. That would be at the end of the financial year of the pools, or of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, which was August 31, 1933. The flax was practically cleaned out. There was no rye held on that date; it had been all sold prior to that. I would have to go through the figures beyond that and ascertain the amounts disposed of month by month.

I am not interested in knowing in what months the grains were sold, but had all the oats been disposed of by December 31, 1934, or by June 30, 1935? Had all the barley been sold and disposed of by, we will say, June 30, 1935?

This report brings the position down to October 31, 1935. Before October 31, 1935, all of the three grains, flax, rye and barley, were disposed of. There were some contracts in connection with oats held at October 31, 1935, and even at this date it would be impossible to say what the final losses might be in that connection or whether they would be as high as they stand now.
I think they have decreased to some extent since this report was prepared. According to this report the loss is $200,000; I think at the present time the loss is really about $188,000, because there have been some transactions in oats since.

The point I want to make clear is as to what the position was at the beginning of October. The order in council is dated October 10 and the offer and acceptance are dated October 8. The statement of the hon. member for Selkirk brings to my mind certain facts which I certainly had not kept in mind; I cannot remember everything. I am curious to know whether the minister can say what the condition -was on October 1, 1935, which will be sufficient for my purpose.

Wheat Board
There are schedules at the end of the report dealing with each one of the grains, and I would have to go through those schedules and select that date, but I can have that information to-morrow.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman could have it by eight o'clock to-night. It becomes important for this reason: Did the sums of money realized from the sale of these oats, barley, rye and flax go to the credit of the companies' accounts in the banks and thereby reduce the guarantee of the country in that connection?
I assume if it were left in its present position that would happen.
I want to know if that is what did happen.

It is all one account, and as I understand it, that one account is guaranteed by the government, but in so far as the books that are kept by the companies are concerned, there are five separate accounts. That is if you are going to pay on the basis of stabilization you must separate those accounts.

The minister has not yet grasped the point of my observation, although the hon. member for Selkirk has done so. Apparently the hon. member has followed this matter with great care, and his statement recalled to my mind a set of facts that otherwise I might not have recalled. The hon. member said-and my colleague from St. Lawrence-St. George said that he had not heard of it before-that as these coarse grains were realized upon the money derived from their sale went to the credit of the account, that is the account in the banks, and thereby decreased the obligation or debt to the banks and, pro tanto, the guarantee of the country. I should like to know to what extent that was so on the first day of October, 1935, for it has a significance to which I shall refer presently.
I will try to get that information. Of course without the amount involved the statement made is correct.
Yes, and if the hon. member for Winnipeg will permit me to say so-
The hon. member for Selkirk.

I was not sure whether my hon. friend or the Minister of Immigration was the representative of Selkirk; I erred in that regard and my hon. friend will have to excuse me. The hon. member for Selkirk made a statement which I think was very
significant, very fair and very clear, if I might be permitted to make that observation without presuming. I cannot agree with his conclusion in law, because the order in council covered wheat only, but as the hon. member was talking about sales of coarse grains he said the understanding was that coarse grains were being taken care of in this order in council; as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was speaking he made the same statement, and I then recalled a circumstance which had escaped my memory entirely. That was that the contention made by the pools, to which the hon. member is now directing attention, was that they, because they had sold coarse grains, should be entitled to receive credit for the amount the country had escaped liability for by reason of the sale of the coarse grains. That matter becomes important, because I have a vague and shadowy recollection of the discussions which took place in regard to that question, and it seems to me that what has been said here this afternoon makes it abundantly clear what the position was. They said, "We have an account at the bank which the country has guaranteed; that account was operated for stabilization and other purposes. You were dealing only with wheat, but as we had only one account all the moneys received from the sale of flax, barley, rye and oats went into that account and thereby reduced the liability of the government." They were endeavouring to say that it was a part of the price they were to receive for the wheat they had on hand that they should be reimbursed the moneys which had come from the sale of coarse grains and had been used to relieve us with respect to that liability. When the hon. member for Selkirk made those statements I recalled at once the contention that was made. It seemed to me then to be not an unsound contention; I agree with what the minister has said, that it is a perfectly sound contention, because last year we were dealing with wheat. If the hon. gentlemen will look at the records of the meetings which took place from time to time they will find that there were suggestions that coarse grains should be dealt with. Finally, the provision as to coarse grains is a permissive provision which comes into force and operation only under certain conditions, and the contention made by the pool directors- there were three of them here^-was that with respect to coarse grains they should get that money because it had gone to reduce the liability which had been guaranteed by the country.

Only for the purpose of arriving at the true wheat balance.
Wheat Board

That is the very point I desired to make, that they said, "If we are going to sell our wheat we want the price of the wheat itself and what money we should receive back either on the acceptance of the liability to the banks or on the added sum."

speechtext: In the form of profits on the coarse grains.

Yes.

When we rose at six
o'clock the minister was good enough to say that he would secure certain information which I required.

With regard to flax,
the information which I have gathered is that the sums which are stated in the report are those that were used in setting up the claim in the first instance, at the time the original order in council was being prepared. On August 31, 1933, the total flax stocks had been disposed of, and on August 31, 1935, there was a surplus of $210,926.05. I assume that if that were to be figured down to the proper amount at October 1, interest would have to be added.

Whatever they were
paying at the bank.

In connection with
rye I wish to say that on August 31, 1933, the total rye stocks had been disposed of, and on August 31, 1935, the rye surplus was $124,276.02. I have not the exact date it was disposed of, but it was some time during the month. At the end of October, 1935, the barley account had been cleaned out. December 2, 1935, the oat stocks had been disposed of. It would appear that the improvement during the month of October would be about in proportion to the quantity sold in November. 238,000	bushels which, by December 2, had been entirely cleaned out.

May I ask a question
with regard to coarse grains? Will the amount of money in the coarse grain pool allow the pools to pay an amount equivalent to the initial payment? I have flax in mind, in connection with which I believe the initial payment was about $1.25. Will the surplus in the pools permit bringing the payments up to that level, or will they be substantially below or above that amount?

The initial payment in the flax pool was one dollar for a time, and seventy-five cents for another period. They had wished to make a payment of $1.25, as a result of the original settlement. The surplus which was mentioned is the amount over and above the initial payments which have already been made. So that that amount is there for distribution. It will not permit of a payment of $1.25, but the amount of money in the pool will provide for a payment somewhere between the present average and $125.
That will be below $1.25?

Yes; it will be below that. I am not sure but that it might be below the dollar, because it is somewhere between seventy-five cents and $125.

Wheat Board
This information may have been given when I was out of the chamber, but I should like to know upon what basis the payment for pool grain is being arranged.
The basis is set out in the bill. I assume the hon. member means payments for wheat.
No, for coarse grains.

In connection with coarse grains we simply return the money to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, and it will be distributed to the pool. We have no control over that; it is really their money.

Like most western members I should like to see this bill passed as quickly as possible, so that this money may go out to the farmers in the west. But some of these documents have been tabled so recently that we have not had access to them. There are some points which are not altogether clear. I notice this afternoon the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Needham) brought up a question which apparently the minister did not quite understand.

speechtext: Oh, no.

I turn1 to page 1456 of
Hansard and I find that the amounts given in the auditor's report are, in round figures, $6,509,000 for wheat, $890,000 for coarse grains, and $862,000 for expenses.
Those are the figures which the auditor's report says were claimed, not the figures which the auditors admit. That was the claim made at the time the order in council was drawn up.

Could we have any idea of the figures which the auditors do admit? My point is this: We have a contract in which the figure of $8,262,000 was agreed to. We have a report submitted and now the minister tells us that a bill is to be brought down to pay somewhere between $6,500,000 and $7,000,000. We cannot understand why there should be this discrepancy between from $6,500,000 to $7,000,000, and $8,262,000, a difference of over $1,500,000, which cannot be entirely accounted for by coarse grains. How is it accounted for? To the best of my understanding this is a contract between the government and the producers of western Canada. I have heard too often hon. gentlemen opposite talking about the sacredness of contracts to believe that they would, tear up a sacred obligation. I can hardly believe that a contract with bankers is sacred whereas an obligation to the farmers is a mere scrap of paper. There must be some explanation and I would like the government to give it.

I will just say in reply that the auditor's report has been tabled and is available to everyone. It will be found, I think, on reading that report and following carefully the legislation that is being brought down, that the legislation provides for the payment of all the money which the auditor's report would permit of our paying. That will be found, I believe, on reading the auditor's report and the legislation itself, and when the case has been fully presented on the second reading of the bill, it will be found that all the money that can properly be paid is being paid under the present legislation.

The point that I last made this afternoon I suppose is answered by the position which the government take that they will not avail themselves of the legislation heretofore passed but propose to have passed a statute of their own. That is,
Wheat Board

of course, within their right, if that is their purpose, but I desire to point out that the law as it now stands would enable them to deal with the situation.
What was said by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) brought to my mind the contentions that were made, namely, that the pools should be reimbursed for the money that had gone to reduce the liability which the government had guaranteed. I find from what the minister says that that sum was not $800,000, but $300,000 odd. I cannot recall at any time having heard the story about oats and that there should be a reimbursement there. The principle on 'which it proceeds I find a little difficult to understand, but that is neither here nor there. The government proposes to make payment for the loss sustained with respect to oats and to return the money that was credited against the guarantee of the government on the sales of flax, rye and barley. I think the pools would also be clearly entitled to the benefit of the interest that the government was released from paying on that account. I do not know what it is or whether it has entered into the computation, but clearly if as a result of the producer's property entrusted to them for sale there has been realized a profit of $300,000, as I understand it, on the basis of the figures mentioned by the minister, there should be a reimbursement for what the country saved by not having to pay interest. That would not be unfair, I should think. With respect to the oats item, I find it a little difficult to follow that in its entirety; indeed, I confess I cannot follow it.
With respect to the matter of expense, that was one of the real difficulties that was responsible for the necessity of introducing a certificate. The report of the auditors on that point has been presented to the government, and so they are able to deal with it. So that leaves no question at issue, if, in the first place, the pools are to be reimbursed the price of wheat on the basis mentioned; and if, in the second place, they are to be reimbursed the moneys to which at least in equity they were entitled, plus the interest saved by reason of its having been credited against the account. That disposes of two questions.
I am unable to deal with oats because I have not grasped the situation in regard to that at all. All I understand is that a loss was made and the country proposes to reimburse the loss.
Probably I could make that clear to the right hon. gentleman.
All right.

The position is this: There are four different accounts, and there are surpluses in three of them. We are returning those surpluses. We had guaranteed those accounts, and we believe that when the account showed a profit we should return the surplus, that is the surplus over and above the initial price paid. So far as oats are concerned there was $200,000 less than enough to pay the initial price paid to the farmer, and our guarantee involves the government paying that $200,000. So, without any provision in this legislation at all we are bound by the guarantee which the government gave to the banks to take care of that $200,000. That goes not to the farmers but to the bank, to pay the losses in connection with that account.
That being a separate account.
Yes.

That makes that abundantly clear. Then, about the fourth item of expenses, there seems to be no difficulty about that. The auditors have reported upon it, and therefore the order in council would still be effective except as to the amount. The amount would be that certified by the auditors, except that in so far as coarse grains are concerned no order in council would be necessary. All the wheat board would have to do would be to repay the amount of money they had received credit for in the accounts of the bank, because when they assumed the bank liability they assumed a liability that had been lessened by the sale of these three commodities, and all that would be necessary would be to issue a cheque for that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They had no authority to do so under the law.
I think they would have, for this is not coarse grains; this is money, and the assumption of liability is an assumption of liability which has been reduced by taking somebody else's property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But where there was a loss-
I quite agree that with respect to losses the position is different, but we do not require any legislation with respect to that because our guarantee covers it, and all we have to do is to pay it.

Legally speaking, we could keep the profits as well; that is to say, our guarantee permits of our keeping them because there is not sufficient money to

Wheat Board
take care of all the government's guarantee. So far as the bank's account is concerned, wheat and everything else are thrown into one account, but there are five different accounts with respect to the farmers.

It does not require legislation to deal with that phase of the matter, nor does it require legislation to deal with respect to losses because we are bound by our guarantee. With respect to expenses, I think that is covered if the expenses are referable to wheat. That must be covered by paragraph (f) of section 7. However, the government has determined to proceed in the other way and not to avail itself of the provisions of the law as it stands, and of course it is their privilege to do so. I was not assenting that parliament could not take any action it pleased with respect to any matter, because parliament is never bound by what has been done. It can always undo what has been done and can do it in some other way. There is a rule of law, to which I might refer, namely, that if you desire to repeal one method and substitute another for it, direct action should be taken. That eliminates the question of implication.
There was a celebrated comment on the law written by Mr. Herbert, one of the great wits of his day, -whose book was highly commended by the Lord Chief Justice of England. He says that there is no such thing as the magna charta because by implication it has been repealed. He then gives the reasons why it has been repealed by implication. That is not very good jurisprudence as it leaves the question whether a statute has been repealed open to implication.
The situation then gets down to this: The government having chosen the method by which to deal with this matter between the producers and the wheat board, it places in the hands of -the wheat board a sum of money which it says they are to pay over to the producers. That is the position as I understand it. What I cannot understand is why a question that was discussed yesterday with such animus could not have been disposed of with the simple statement that the addition to the original conception of the order in council was made with no political consideration. It must be apparent to anyone who goes into the matter at all that that must be the case when you add to any proposal a condition that subjects its operation to a delay that must be inevitable, namely, the auditor's receipt. I looked up some of the newspapers published at that time and I found a long article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of October 10. It seems that at that time there
was no doubt. There was a statement that this was the correct understanding of it. The article reads:
The Free Press Wednesday asked W. F. McLeod, prominent pool official when the payments would be made. Mr. McLeod said there was no truth whatever in the report. "Its a damned lie,'' he said, "and you can tell that to whoever told the Free Press."
That is very strong language to use in dealing with the matter. The question as to the eighth and- tenth of October being important dates wras raised and someone suggested that there must have been very speedy facilities for the transportation of mail between Winnipeg and Ottawa. Surely it must be known to the hon. member who mentioned the matter that in the very necessity of things much of this would be discussed by telephone. The reason this matter was dealt with was the fact that the pool was clamouring to get rid of its wheat and to hand over its obligations at the banks to the new wheat board, and the new wheat board was endeavouring to commence its operations. Before it was able to do so, solicitors had to be consulted and the forms had to be prepared. This involved much delay and in all that time the government was dealing with the problem of fixing prices. At the same time it was negotiating for a basis upon which these assets of the producers could be turned over to the new wheat board. These terms had to be embodied in some form of contract and ultimately the contract took the form of an offer and an acceptance in writing. The government had to approve and decide upon such ;erms and conditions as might be agreed upon with the approval of the governor in council. When the matter came to the government I remember I was not here. I have looked it up and I find that on those days I was in Cornwall, Lindsay and Toronto. I well recall Mr. Hunter coming to me and I well recall the report being presented to me. I recall also writing into the document the provision that there should be a verification of the amounts by an auditor's certificate.
If one looks up what took place in 1930 he will find that one rather important matter was never completed because of delay in getting the order in council circulated in time to have it signed by the fourth man. An appointment which might have been made was never made. That is an indication of what might happen in connection with questions of this kind. Why it should be suggested that there was anything sinister behind it, or why it should be left to inference that there was something dishonourable in connection with it, I eamiot for the
Wheat Board

life of me understand. I should like to have it made abundantly clear to this committee before it rises whether o-r not this government charges the late administration with any sinister purpose or any fraudulent design or improper procedure in endeavouring to carry out the transactions to which reference has been made to-day.
Mr. GARDiINER: I may say that I think the inference that something of that kind might be taken from the remarks of either myself or others has been largely on the part of my hon. friends opposite. I have criticized the means by which the order in council was developed and by which signature was obtained to the order in council.
Whose?

I have not said at any
time that there was any sinister motive or anything of that kind in connection with it. I am quite sure that no member of the government thinks there was any sinister motive. There might have been a political motive, but that is something the people will have to decide for themselves. I do not think anyone has suggested or insinuated that there has been any sinister motive or any disposing of the funds of Canada in an improper manner. I -am quite free to say this to the leader of the opposition. I think probably I have said most of what has been said on the part of the government, that there was no such intention in connection with any part of it. There was the pointing out of the fact that this did take place in the week immediately preceding the election and there was some reason why there might be difficulty in having ministers present at that particular time. The only fact which might require a little explaining is, -as t-o why it should have been done in that week. While that might require some explanation, there is nothing sinister involved. It is simply a matter of choice on the part of the government as to when this should be done.

I am obliged to the minister for that statement. I should like to make clear that even political motives cannot be attached to this transaction. When the order in council was issued it provided that it would not become effective until an auditor's certificate had been provided and that could not be done between the date of the order in council and the date of the elections. Of course it follows that you never can convince those who are your political opponents that anything you do is done with other than political motives. That being so, I suppose it is equally true that those who now sit to the left of the Chairman view

the acts of the present administration as having behind them political motives. When one sees that they take steps that their opponents might have hesitated to take with the same means, one wonders whether, after all, political motives are not attached by all opponents to governments in power, whatever they may do, good, bad or indifferent. That, I think, is fairly apparent from what has been said here, but I was deeply hurt that it should be suggested in the terms in which it was yesterday that this matter had behind it something that was very improper. Why should we have had all this discussion when a single sentence would have answered the whole matter, namely, that the delay was due to the fact that it had been provided in the order in council that an auditor's certificate should be forthcoming before payments were made; that that certificate was not available on the 25th of January, and that when it was it did not warrant payment being made in the amount specified in the order in council?

Now.
Is it printed?

Last evening I asked for the permission of the house to have the bill read the second time, if possible, so that we might proceed with it, and I am informed-I say this for the information of the leader of the opposition-that everything has been done to get the bill in readiness for the presses to start immediately the first reading is given, so that copies will be got out right away and distributed as soon as it is possible to get them here. Reserving those rights, and without prejudice, I certainly offer no objection to the bill being read the second time.

Carried.
I wish to make some remarks-
That is rather difficult unless we have copies of the bill.
With permission for me to make, in the committee stage or following that, the address that would be made on second reading, I think that is satisfactory.
Quite so.
I do not think we ought to be asked to pass the second reading of the bill without having copies of it before us.
The second reading has been carried.
I do not see much advantage in proceeding inasmuch as we cannot go into committee without the bill.
You can get the second reading.

speechtext: Second reading! It is possible only by unanimous consent, and if my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) objects, of course the bill cannot now be read the second time.
The second reading was passed before he objected.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the guarantee by the government of Canada of the principal and interest of loans made to or guaranteed by the province of Saskatchewan for purchasing seed grain and providing other assistance to farmers in connection with seeding operations during the spring of 1936.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacMillan in the chair.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Will the minister explain this, as to the amount involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The question of seed grain has been a vital one on many occasions in the history of western Canada, and various measures have been necessary from time to time, on the part of both provincial and federal governments, to deal with it. During the past season very considerable damage by rust was caused in Saskatchewan and in parts of the other provinces as well, with the result that the grain was so much damaged as to be no good for seed. This has created a very serious problem, much more serious in Saskatchewan than in either of the other provinces, and the measure for which this resolution is the foundation is designed to cooperate with Saskatchewan in meeting this situation.
The province has on its statute books certain legislation respecting loans by municipalities and by local improvement districts, under the terms of which statutes borrowings by local authorities are guaranteed by the province. The legislation which will be based upon the resolution now under consideration involves adding the federal government's guarantee to that of the province with respect to obtaining loans for the purposes indicated. The amount which will be found in the bill as the aggregate principal amount which may be guaranteed by its terms is $4,000,000. While under the terms of the resolution the federal government guarantees repayment of principal and interest, provision is made in the bill to the effect that if the federal government should be called upon to implement its guarantee with respect to any portion of the amounts advanced, Saskatchewan must reimburse the federal government in that amount, or must deliver to the finance minister securities of that province representing the amount of money which the federal government is called upon to pay. Three years is allowed in the legislation-this is :a detail which I suppose should be explained at a later stage, but I want to give a general understanding of the situation-with respect to implementing any guarantee under the legislation.
I think that is all I have to say at the moment. The measure can be, naturally, very much better understood when it is before hon. members at later stages, but I desire to convey at this stage a fairly complete appreciation of what it is because of the fact, of course, that it is entirely a financial measure.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Is this legislation in Saskatchewan new legislation at the recent session, or does it follow the lines of the legislation passed in Saskatchewan last year, which-

Seed Grain

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: The hon. member is speaking of the provincial legislation?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Yes-which guaranteed the loan companies? Does this guarantee the loan companies, or does it guarantee the local authorities? In other words, is this a variation from the legislation of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: The provincial legislation as amended this year is entitled "An act to enable municipalities to borrow money for the distribution of seed grain and supplies." I have gone through it very carefully in order to reply with accuracy to my hon. friend. The legislation of Saskatchewan relates to municipalities, and there is a separate statute relating to local improvement districts, in which the matter is being handled this year in a slightly different manner from that in which it was handled last year, inasmuch as under the Local Improvement District Act as amended this year the minister of municipal affairs of the province becomes the borrower.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Is the rate of interest specified?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: No; there is no rate of interest specified in the bill. One of the primary objects of the federal guarantee is to ensure the lowest possible rate of interest from the banks for loans of this kind.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question which affects the principle as indicated in this resolution? Instead of making loans or guaranteeing loans and interest, have the government considered the advisability of making a loan to the province or to any other distributing authority of the actual wheat now in their possession? The wheat in their possession costs money to carry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: A good deal of it is being carried in privately owned elevators, terminals owned by private companies, upon which there is a regular carrying charge of approximately, I think, a cent a month. It strikes me that if we could loan the wheat, with the understanding that out of the crops grown a return could be made of this seed wheat, this might be better than handling the matter in a financial way and guaranteeing loans and paying interest. Would the minister say whether that suggestion has been considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Yes. It occurred to my own imagination that there might possibly be some merit in working it out in that way, and I had an examination made of the possi-

bilities of it through the wheat board and also through the provincial authorities. But the complications were entirely too great. This procedure seems to be much more simple, and in relation to the wheat itself, which is now owned by the wheat board, naturally the wheat board, or those acting for the wheat board in the country elevators, will be the suppliers of the wheat, and the wheat which is supplied will constitute a sale on the part of the wheat board to the municipality, or to the local improvement district, as the case may be, and will thus immediately stop storage charges as far as that particular wheat is concerned. In other words, this method of accomplishing the purpose is merely machinery designed to effect the end that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) desires to see effected.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Except in this one regard. If the money is borrowed by a municipality or the province or some other authority, it will be borrowed, in all probability, from the banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: And interest will be paid to the banks for the loan of such money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Then, that money will in turn be used to purchase wheat from the wheat board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
On the other hand if the wheat board-and they have wheat scattered all over the country; they have some in Edmonton, some in Saskatoon, some at Moose Jaw, some at the head of the lakes, some at Vancouver, some in Lethbridge; it is all) over the country-could loan the wheat, it strikes me that the machinery would not be different. Then the borrower could receive the loan, but instead of receiving it in value upon which he pays interest, he could receive the loan of the wheat and this would save him the interest. It may be said that that is unwise, because the government would be getting no interest, but the government is now paying interest to the banks for the carrying charges of the wheat, particularly the futures' contracts that are held. It is all the same; it has the same effect. It is paying charges to elevator companies for carrying this wheat, some of which, I venture to say, that is now owned by the government or the wheat board, has been held for four years. I think some of it still is being carried on the old contracts

Seed Grain
of four years ago and has cost in carrying charges about forty cents a bushel. That is one of the tragedies of carrying this wheat. My suggestion is that if we lend the wheat we could save the farmer whatever little interest charge is involved-it does not amount to much, but it is something-we could save the government or the wheat board the carrying charges of that wheat during the time, one year or whatever period it is, that the farmer would have to use it, and the farmer could return the wheat next fall by a deduction from whatever he delivers of the amount of seed he received, provided of course he has a reasonable crop.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: That is the trouble.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Well, then, this can be spread over a period of two or three years. This practice of making monetary loans for the purpose of seed grain purchases is a very old one in this country. I venture to say that in the last three or four months my hon. friends in their treasury board have cancelled scores of old accounts, some ten, fifteen and twenty years old, in respect of advances made years and years ago in this way. On the other hand, if we ultimately lost the wheat it certainly would not be a larger proportion than we are now losing on cash loans that have been made, and I think it would be a much better system of handling the matter than making cash loans. I cannot understand why we should create a considerable fund-$4,000,000 is suggested; I admit it is not a very large sum, but it is $4,000,000-and pay interest to banks on that sum, merely to advance credit. When we have the wealth right in our own hands and do not know what to do with it, why not work out a system under which you could loan the wheat itself?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether Manitoba has applied for a similar loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Manitoba has been advised of the conditions of this legislation and is at liberty to apply for similar assistance if it is required, but I am advised that that province expects to be able to care for its requirements otherwise. The area in Manitoba that is affected is relatively limited, and while what I say is subject to change if we are differently advised, according to my advice at the moment Manitoba expects to be able to look after its own requirements.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Why does not the government proceed by order in council under the 12739-96i
relief act, as we did last year in connection with seed grain for Saskatchewan and Alberta? By order in council dated May 31, 1935, with regard to Alberta and order in council dated April 8, 1935, in regard to Saskatchewan, instead of guaranteeing it, the money was loaned to the provinces and they dealt with the matter themselves. As far as we are concerned surely the statute is broad enough to enable the matter to be dealt with in that way, so why is it not dealt with by order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Frankly, we believe that this is a better method of dealing with the matter, principally as a result of past experience in the province itself. The best results ever secured in the administration of seed grain came about as a consequence of the adoption of this policy, and when I say the best results I mean from the standpoint of repayment by the farmers. The farmers felt their obligation to their municipality, which was their own local, self-governing entity, and apparently made much greater efforts in the way of repayment than ever before had been the case in connection with advances of the kind mentioned a few moments ago by my hon. friend from East Kootenay. Such advances were made many years ago and, as the hon. member says, from time to time in the treasury board it is necessary to write them off. The experience in that regard may be interesting.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: But that would not be changed; that practice was in foroe last year. The amounts advanced to Saskatchewan last year were dealt with in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: You mean loaned directly from the federal treasury?

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: Certainly. You are giving guarantees, and it is the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: I am anxious to get the resolution through, and I desire not to say anything which will give even the slightest offence to my right hon. friend.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Even since this session began millions of dollars have been advanced to Saskatchewan under the relief act which parliament passed last year. The provision is there to deal with such matters; the law is there, it was passed last year. This year you are going to deal with the matter differently; you are going to pass a statute. Everything you could do by statute you can do by order in council. Even in the last six weeks you have been dealing with millions of dollars in connection with the four western prov-
Seed Grain

inoes. I have the list before me, showing $3,000,000 at a time in connection with Saskatchewan. Why did we not pass a statute in respect of those amounts?

Certainly, but with this
blank cheque which you condemned so roundly; you utilized that to increase the grants to the provinces without regard to need at all, with no need test at all. The grants to all the provinces, Prince Edward Island, British Columbia, Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and all the others, were increased to seventy-five per cent. I stand subject to correction as to whether the figure is seventy-five per cent, but that is my memory according to the statement of the Prime Minister the other day. During the last six weeks, with parliament in session, the government has been dealing with loans to Saskatchewan. I have before me the list of renewals and new loans to Alberta, Manitoba, British Columbia and so on; almost every few days an order in council is laid on the table of the house, and this morning I took the trouble to look at them. When you can deal with this whole situation through the municipalities, just as we did last year, with the province assuming the responsibility, under the legislation passed last year, why are we having recourse to a statute in this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I suppose I must be prepared for a fight. I simply say frankly that this is definitely a part of the policy of the present government to get rid of that very method of which my right hon. friend is speaking. I will be quite frank; one of the things quite appalling to me, returning to the office of finance minister after five years, is the extent of power under the statute to which my right hon. friend refers. I recognize that there was very grave necessity, in many instances, for power to act, but the breadth and extent of use, and the tremendous sums of money involved in what has come to be called the blank cheque system, constitute a very grave responsibility for a finance minister to carry. My right hon. friend says that we have been using that authority. Surely there can be no question about this: Prior to the assembling of parliament there

was no other authority under which it was possible for the government to act in order to renew obligations already existing, and to take care of conditions, particularly with respect to relief, as they arose.
My right hon. friend says that we increased the payments to the provinces on account of direct relief without any need test; I think that was the word he used. I suggest that he might credit us with having very carefully examined that situation and having examined also his own method of dealing with it. In fact his method of dealing with direct relief was not changed. The question of the adequacy of the then existing scale of payment to meet conditions which we found existing in many of our major municipalities during the past winter brought the government to the conclusion that the increase was essential in order to put the people of this country through the winter. We had the authority under the legislation to which my right hon. friend refers. We had no parliament in session. We used the authority that was there, and I submit that we had no alternative.
Now, since parliament has met, surely the only complaint that can be made is that this type of legislation has not been introduced at an earlier date in order to get out from under the necessity of the blank cheque, as far as possible and as quickly as possible. Perhaps there is some ground for that criticism. It is really a question for a government to determine at the opening of a session of parliament as to which are the first things in importance to be dealt with, to be presented to parliament in session. We used our very best judgment in determining which were the first things, and we think we put first things first. But gradually, as the session progresses, we are endeavouring to replace the order in council provisions, under the statutes to which reference has been made, by statutes enacted in this parliament giving specific and requisite authority with respect to these matters. In times like these, of course, certain latitude is required. My own difference with my right hon. friend would be the extent to which he took that power to the government. I believe it really went beyond the necessities of the situation, great though they were, and it is important that parliament should retain in its own hands control over great expenditures and the manner in which they are made. The subject is a difficult one. My right hon. friend knows better than any other man in this house the difficulties I am facing in connection with these very matters, because he has experienced them. At the same time we are desir-

ous of having parliamentary authority with respect to matters which, as my right hon. friend correctly states, could to-day be dealt with by order in council under existing legislation. I have tried to be as non-provocative as possible in discussing the question, because I desire to make some headway.

Five days from to-day the relief act is no longer in force. It expires on March 31, 1936. Thus far no provision, other than the resolution endeavouring to deal with Saskatchewan, has been made to deal with any problems. I am pointing out that if this is necessary with respect to Saskatchewan, between now and five days from now the power to deal with Alberta and Manitoba will have gone. It is no use suggesting that they may come in, because this house will rise a week from Wednesday for twelve days, and unless there is some statute which may be made effective, the government will have no power to deal with the matter. I suggest that if we are going to single out Saskatchewan to the extent of over S4,000,000, the proper course would have been to make some provision through which the government- could also have dealt with the other provinces. Place a limitation upon it, if you like, and do it by statute, if you will. I would not complain if the government did it by statute, if in the exercise of its discretion it feels it preferable to deal with the matter in that way, rather than by order in council. But it can only deal with it by order in council within the next five days.
I was hopeful that at least something might be done to enable the critical situation in some provinces other than Saskatchewan to be dealt with. I have mo objection in the world to the government following that out in any way it pleases, because in view of the denunciations which took place during the last three or four years I had expected that in the first week of parliament the relief act would have been repealed, and that a new provision would have been offered to deal with the situation. The minister did not catch the point of my criticism with respect to a general increase without a need test, because every province was not in the same position. But every province shared to the same extent in the increase. I know of my own knowledge, before leaving office, exactly
what the position was in some of the provinces in connection with what they had to do monthly for their own relief, and how wholly more than adequate in some cases and how wholly inadequate in other cases it might be.
