speechtext:
I should not like the subject I introduced a moment ago to be brushed aside too lightly. I am not personally concerned about the exact method used to perform this particular task. I have no objection to the resolution, but I am desirous of pointing out to the committee that if the resolution passes in its present form, and no consideration is given to the other suggestion, then such suggestion is swept aside and not considered at all.
Before I desist from bringing it to the attention of the minister I should like once again to emphasize the significance of the matter. This guarantee of loans amounting to $4,000,000 will in all probability be substantially absorbed. I believe we could say that it would be taken up in full. That means that there would be $160,000 per annum interest, taking the rate of four per cent. If it were done the other way there would be no need whatever of paying $160,000 interest. Mark you, the security is just such things as we have, namely the wheat in our elevators. We have about 200,000,000 bushels of wheat in our elevators, and that is real wealth; in fact it is better wealth than the currency of our country. It has real value. That physical grain could be loaned to the farmers without interest and with no loss to the government. On the contrary there would be a saving of elevator and carrying charges. I am not criticizing the minister, because this has been done before, but I would say to him that we are proposing to saddle ourselves with a guarantee of interest. We are asking

the producers to pay the interest, and as I say, in the aggregate it would amount to around $160,000 a year, running for a period of three years. There we have about a half a million dollars in interest alone, and in my opinion there is no need to incur that interest debt.
The minister stated that there was a question of machinery to be considered. May I suggest to the minister how it could be done without interfering with in the slightest degree, or without losing the advantage of the so-called machinery which has been set up. I assume that in the present instance the government would simply give a guarantee, and that in all probability the provinces would be the agencies handling the matter. They would handle it, downwards, by distribution through the municipalities, and would buy wheat from the wheat board. Instead of buying the wheat from the wheat board, paying to the wheat board a cheque which we guarantee, why not let the province go to the wheat board and borrow its wheat and get, not a warehouse receipt because it is the reverse of a warehouse receipt, but a document admitting the borrowing of so much wheat which has to be returned, or returned in value, at a given time. My good friend the Minister of Finance is smiling, but I really see no difficulty in the matter at all, and with the government having in its possession through the wheat board a couple of hundred million bushels of wheat I can see no reason in the world why we should not loan it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
I was not smiling in any offensive way, I assure my hon. friend, but surely if his proposal has any financial or economic merit it rests wholly upon his statement with respect to the saving of interest charges. It cannot rest upon the saving of storage charges because, of course, storage will not be paid on the wheat after it is taken out by the farmer to be sown. What my hon. friend forgets in respect to the interest is this fact, that the wheat board would have to go on paying interest to the banks on that money. My hon. friend's proposition would really mean that the wheat board would be loaning wheat to the farmers free of interest, but that does not mean that there would be no interest paid, because the wheat board has borrowed the money wherewith to acquire the wheat in the first place, and if it has sold the wheat without repaying its loan it would have to continue paying interest on the money. I am not criticizing my hon. friend for falling into that little error because I did so myself at first in examining this matter.

Seed Grain
With regard to mechanical difficulties may I point out that the distribution of that wheat from, the point at which it presently is to the point at which it is needed has to be paid for by somebody. If the loan is to be a loan in kind with repayment in kind, there must be a translation in some manner of the money cost of movement into terms of wheat. That is another little complication, and one which is not without its difficulty in practical application. I can assure my hon. friend that when I got through with a complete examination of all that was involved it was rather difficult to see that any saving would be effected for anybody by adopting the suggestion which he has made.

If my hon. friend
remembers the provisions of the Wheat Board Act of last session he will remember that prior to the time when the wheat board takes delivery of any wheat it is being financed by the agents of the wheat board, who are the pools and the elevator companies throughout the west. It is being financed by them in the ordinary way in their own country elevator storage, and the wheat board takes delivery-I do not know that it must take delivery even in the terminals, but that is where it takes delivery in any event-and the wheat is then paid for by the wheat board with funds which are loans from banks under the guarantee of the government of Canada. My hon. friend, of course, knows that a very large portion of the holdings from stabilization account, and so forth, are represented by future contracts and not by actual wheat delivered, and in that respect a bank loan is necessary which is guaranteed by the government with respect to the clearing house accounts of the wheat board from time to time.

subsubtopic: GUARANTEE OP LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext: All I wish to add is that I understood from Mr. McFarland himself some two years ago that he was taking delivery of considerable quantities of wheat, taking title to it and paying for it. I do not think it was a very substantial portion of the whole holdings, but it was a considerable quantity, and one of the considerations was this, and I might as well mention it now: It had been the practice for a long time to carry practically all this wheat in company elevators, while we had the Moose Jaw elevator idle, almost empty, and almost every other government elevator empty. I think the one at Lethbridge has some one hundred thousand bushels in it, with a capacity of over one million bushels, and the Port Arthur elevator was nearly empty for years. I myself suggested and urged that we should use government elevator facilities for the storage of the wheat, instead of constantly paying storage to the company elevators as we were doing. As my hon. friend knows perhaps better than any other man in the house, the elevator companies for the last five or six years have been making most of their money out of the storage of wheat.

I believe I am not far wrong. They have been making a handsome profit at all events through carrying wheat in private storage- private, I mean, in the sense of ownership, because they are public terminals privately owned-and they were making this money while our own elevators were empty. I remember very well discussing this matter with Mr. McFarland, suggesting that we had abundant space and urging that we should load up our own elevators. This question of contracts came up, and I suggested that we might as well take delivery and store the wheat in our own elevators and save paying storage. I assume that we have a considerable quantity of that wheat, and it seems to me that if we have taken delivery and the title rests in the dominion government in the right of the wheat board we might very well afford to loan the wheat out rather than continue the method of paying storage to private elevators. subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
At the outset, may I say that I approve the general principle of this bill, and that I have great admiration for the Minister of Marine (Mr. Howe), who is bringing in the measure. I believe that in Vancouver he is regarded as a minister of exceptional ability and fairness. 1 do suggest, however, that there should be in the bill some provision for the appointment or election of advisory local councils. That may not be so necessary in the case of ports that are near Ottawa, but I suggest that there should be at least the power to appoint or to elect such a local advisory council. That recommendation has been made by Sir Alexander Gibb in his very able report, and I would refer the minister to page 4, paragraph 9, in which Sir Alexander says:
Adequate representation of local interests and of the port users, which at present is almost non-existent, is essential to the progress and efficiency of a port, and a strong local harbour council should be established on an elective basis.

The idea is, I imderstand, that such council should serve without remuneration. A local advisory council would be particularly helpful to the port of Vancouver for the following reasons. That port is very far removed from Ottawa and it will be very difficult for a central control board to keep in touch with the problems of the port; further, there is bound to be delay in handling those problems. Then, the port is the only one on the Pacific coming under the terms of this act; our problems are those of a Pacific port and not of a port on the Atlantic or on the St. Lawrence. I suggest to the minister that the problems are quite different and are those of the ports of Seattle and Portland, with which we are in direct and strenuous competition. Again, private business interests have had far more to do with the development of Vancouver than is the case with these other national ports.
Again, I refer to the report of Sir Alexander Gibb, quoting from page 178:
I feel inclined to emphasize the tendency of Vancouver to develop on rather different lines from those of other dominion ports, in that there is there a much greater participation of private enterprise. Vancouver is a national port and its policy must be directed accordingly, but so long as local business continues to play the part in its development that it does at present, it should be given full scope, subject only to the overruling considerations of the national policy.
That is a direct finding on this particular question which I am discussing to-night.
We have in Vancouver a port manager who is an excellent man; he knows the port and the work; but managing that port is very big business, and it is physically impossible for a port manager to keep in contact with the various groups using the port. Sir Alexander Gibb also realized this point, and I would quote from page 31 of the report:
Considerable latitude should be allowed to the port managers, so long as their activities are directed to carrying out the policy laid down by the central authority. It is essential to avoid emasculating the local administration, since no centralized control can replace an efficient and active local administration, or the special knowledge and initiative of the local business community, both of which are vital to a port's prosperity.
Then he goes on:
For this reason I strongly advocate a local advisory council. There are very many aspects of port working which such a council can properly care for, such as the representation of the interests of private wharf owners, of local merchants and distributors, of local consignees and exporters, of the labour view, and of the attitude of boards of trade, chambers of commerce, corn exchanges and other such trade organizations, in addition to shipping.

National Harbours Board-Mr. Ryan
It serves very usefully to identify the community with the port; and to secure the support and interest of local members of parliament, the city council, or provincial government in schemes, and so anticipate and meet criticisms from any such quarters, or action that might be prejudicial to the port.
It is invaluable in exploring the possibilities of local markets, in carrying out advertisement and propaganda, and in cooperation with interests likely to promote industrial developments. Finally, a local council provides a useful check on the tendency of more or less permanent officials to become stereotyped or arbitrary.
I cannot emphasize this too strongly, because our port is vital to the development of Vancouver. Sir Alexander goes on;
The port manager would be ex officio chairman of the council, which would meet regularly and be consulted on all such matters as proposed developments, alterations in rates, important changes in operation. The members of the council should have the right of initiating discussions on matters of policy affecting the port, on any complaints raised by users of the port, and on questions of rates, charges, etc.; but not on any purely executive matters, and they would have no executive duties or powers.
The advisory council's proceedings and recommendations would be submitted to the central authority, and they should have the right of direct access to the central authority, but not to any other department of government.
I suggest to the minister that without a local council of some sort there is bound to be misunderstanding, there is bound to be friction in a port so far removed from Ottawa as is the port of Vancouver.
In closing, may I say that I have every confidence that the minister is trying to do the right thing for all of our great national ports, but I hope that he will consider again this question of appointing or electing local advisory councils. I cannot too strongly or too earnestly impress upon both the minister and the members of the house the need of such a council in the case of the port of Vancouver.

speechtext:
I want to make a few comments on this bill, since it affects the port of Saint John. Saint John was in a unique position among the ports of this country in that it owned its port prior to the sale to the dominion government in 1917. It assisted in the development of the port by the expenditure of large sums of money; it owned the fisheries; it owned the lands underneath the water. As all these things belonged to the city, certain reservations were asked for when the port was sold to the dominion government, and these reservations are contained in the act which set up the harbour commission for the port of Saint John.
The present bill makes no particular reference to the port of Saint John except in two instances. Section 6 refers to bringing the port under the jurisdiction of the new harbour commissioners, and section 39 provides for the repeal of the act to set up the Saint John harbour commission. I wish to call to the attention of the hon. minister that the city of Saint John, when it sold its port to the dominion government, asked for certain reservations, and those reservations are contained in the act of 1927, chapter 67, 17 George V. Section 17 of the act states:
The fisheries lots now the property of the city are to remain under the control of the city authorities until such time as said lots or any part thereof may be required for public purposes, and possession of the whole or any part thereof shall be yielded up to the use and control of the corporation after six months on the serving of notice to that effect in writing by the corporation on the city.
The section goes on further;
Likewise there is to be reserved to the city the right to use, for ferry purposes, the following property:-
And it sets out the boundaries which it reserves to the city for a certain time as specified in the section itself for use for ferry purposes. I am not going to deal with the boundaries, but I call attention to the fact that after the description of the boundaries it is stated that the city shall have the use of those boundaries-to read from the section-
[DOT]-until the Canadian National Railways or any government authority shall construct a bridge across, or tunnel under any part of the harbour not farther north or west than Hilyard's reef and Navy island,-or at such other point as may be agreed to by the city,- by which provision shall be made for a street railway service and free accommodation for foot passenger and other vehicular service; then and in such case, the city shall convey to the Crown the said lands and rights above reserved. In the meantime, the city shall be responsible for the maintenance of the property, so reserved, in its present condition at its own expense.
I submit that if this bill is passed in its present form-and provision is made here for the repeal of the original act; therefore those reservations which were reserved to the city of Saint John will be a fortiori repealed as well-this may lead to considerable difficulties at the port of Saint John. For that reason I call these particular sections to the attention of the minister. It may be said that in the bill before the house section 37 may be described as a saving section, but in my opinion that section will not help to iron out the difficulties which will ensue if the bill goes through in its present form resulting in the entire repeal of the original act which set up the Saint John harbour commission.

National Harbours Board-Mr. Ryan
Section 37 of the bill before the house states:
The corporations and the board are hereby declared to be amalgamated and to form one corporation under the name of the "National Harbours Board" which shall possess and be vested with all the works and undertakings and all other the powers, rights, privileges, franchises, assets, effects and properties, real, personal and mixed, belonging to, possessed by, or vested in each of the corporations at or before the coming into force of this act-
And so on. That section cannot be of any assistance, I submit, so far as Saint John is concerned, because under the act which set up the Saint John harbour commission no real estate was vested in the Saint John harbour board; it had only the management and control of the property, and if reference is made to the act itself it will be found that all real estate is vested in His Majesty the King. I saw the original deed and I know that is the way it is made out; as a matter of fact the act provides that it shall be made out in that way. So I call these particular sections to the attention of the hon. minister. I do not want to delay the passage of this resolution, but I think at this time these matters should be referred to, and if the minister will look into these different sections it may facilitate matters when the bill is before the committee. I think every section of the original act should be carefully scrutinized and analyzed before this house is asked to repeal that measure which set up the Saint John harbour commission. Unless this is done it may lead to very great difficulties; it may result in lawsuits, and in any case it will leave matters in a condition in which they should not be left having regard to the original legislation.
I am not here to oppose the principle of the bill; if the minister thinks it will be in the interests not only of the port of Saint John but of all Canada to have these different ports brought under one management, so far as I am concerned I am prepared to give this a fair trial. Like the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) who spoke on this bill previously, I am a little apprehensive as well in regard to what the hon. member described as the long arm management directing affairs from the capital city in respect to transportation and similar matters affecting our port of Saint John, but I have absolute confidence in the minister himself. He is a man of experience, an engineer, familiar with marine matters and transportation, and we will look to him to see that the port of Saint John is protected after this bill is put into effect. Let me repeat, however, that I hope he will have this bill care-
fully scrutinized before it gets to the committee, because in its present form this bill will repeal many sections of the original act which were placed there especially to protect the interests of the port of Saint John.

speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker
and hon. members, for the privilege you have extended in permitting me to speak to-night without regard for a technicality which might have prevented me from so doing. I would have continued when I moved the adjournment of the debate last Tuesday night had it not been for the fact that for the past ten or twelve days I have been confined to my bed, unable to attend the sittings of the house. I had the good fortune, however, to be present that Tuesday evening and to hear one or two of the speeches, including that of my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett).
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I have read all the sections of the bill that has been introduced by the hon. Minister of Marine and Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Transport to be. I agree with a great many of the points mentioned by the right hon. leader of the opposition in his masterly speech the other evening, when he made comparisons between the various ports and mentioned the futility, as he put it, of attempting to develop certain ports that neither God nor nature had ever intended to be such. Happily for me, sir, I come from a province that adjoins that in which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition was born. In those little provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island were bom, I think, those finer ideals that are exemplified today in the confederation of this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
Much was promised to the little province of Nova Scotia in the early days. Great were

National Harbours Board-Mr. Finn
our hopes and wonderful our ambitions, I well remember as a lad hearing the late Hon.
A.	G. Jones and my late uncle, Doctor Edward Farrell, who were great contenders for Liberalism in the historic constituency of Halifax against the late Mr. John F. Stairs and the late Mr. T. E. Kenny. I remember my uncle coming in through the proscenium wings of the old academy of music and starting to speak. At once he put his hand to *his ear and said, "Hark, do you hear the whistle of the Hongkong train? No, and why? Because it is blowing in Portland." It may be that we who have to deal with measures involving the future development of Canada both east and west are not in a more happy position because, while the whistle of the Hongkong train is not blowing in Portland, I can assure hon. members that a great many of the ships that go up the St. Lawrence to Quebec and Montreal do not make their terminus at either Halifax or Saint John when the Almighty closes navigation on that great river for five or six months of the year.
I am a proud supporter of the present government, whose leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) I follow with an allegiance amounting almost to a religious belief, because he has followed in the footsteps of that great Canadian the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who had no equal with the possible exception of the Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald. Possibly if the right hon. leader of the opposition lives long enough, as I hope he will, and learns as he lives, he may qualify for such companionship in the future. I desire to remind the house that the government of the right hon. Prime Minister brought to Canada Sir Andrew Rae Duncan who, with Professor Macmillan of McGill university and the late Judge W. B. Wallace of Halifax, were a royal commission created to deal with the great transportation problem of this dominion, and to determine whether it was possible to keep within the confines of Canada and on Canadian soil our great products until they reach the great harbours east and west from which, sail great ships over the seven seas.
The report of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan-an outstanding man; otherwise he would not have come to Canada-advised the formation of harbour boards, and also advised the construction of facilities in order that the provinces nearest the sea might be in a position to cope with the trade that was to be carried over the great transcontinental railways, of which Canada has at least four to-day. In compliance with the recommendations of that report the government of the right hon. the present Prime Minister created harbour commissioners and laid down rules and regulations. They were under the able administration of the then Minister of Marine, the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin). Under that legislation all capital expenditures were referred to Ottawa, and properly so.
It is said that "while the lamp holds out to burn, the vilest sinner may return." The right hon. the leader of the opposition, knowing of its successful operation when he was Prime Minister, When he qpoke paid great compliments to the two chairmen of his commission, Mr. Phinney, K.C., and Mr. Hether-ington, both appointed by himself. He spoke with the Gibb report in his hands, recommending abolition of commissions, and the appointment of port managers for every port in Canada; yet he disregarded it then, and now he praises it.
To-night I wish to compliment the Minister of Railways and Canals and Minister of Marine (Mr. Howe) upon his appointment. He has brought to the office skill of a type which few hon. members possess, and intelligence and youth, although he has not so much of that which grows on the top of the head. It would not take an accountant very long to count them, even if I stopped for five minutes to permit him so to do.

speechtext:
May I say to the hon. member that if it is a question of sour grapes, the next time I pay a . compliment I will extend it to him. When I was interrupted I was referring to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and to the introduction of this legislation which carries with it the sanction of the government and, of course, the sanction of supporters of the government if it is to survive. Liberal governments are always ready to listen to reasonable, understandable and explainable amendments, and an open discussion of a bill is in order, so that the people may know what is taking place.
I understand that Sir Alexander Gibb advised doing away with harbour commissioners, and the appointment of harbour managers and a system of central control which would work out to the financial benefit of the country, and would have the effect of removing from politics those matters which to-day are the inevitable subjects of discussion, if politicians are to exist. If they are not to exist no hon. member would have the right to enter this chamber.
I have given in the past a great deal of study to the development of the port of Halifax and to the reduction of freight rates. I have argued before the railway commission
1512	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Finn
and before ,the Supreme Court of Canada on questions of law reserved by the railway sommission in connection with the Crows-nest pass agreement. Unfortunately, under the bill it seems to me that too much authority is placed, not in the hands of the Minister of Transport to be: but in those of a board to be created, with headquarters at Ottawa and which would operate all harbours from one end of Canada to the other. To a major degree it would control and take away that autonomy about which the right hon. the leader of the opposition spoke on Tuesday night.
I have never been a believer in absent treatment, and I would not be in my place to-night if I had depended upon surgeons treating me over the telephone. If they had not come alongside the operating table and attended to my case, as they did at the time of diagnosis, it would not have been well for me. Absent treatment can never be a success, because there is not present a specialist with the ability to apply the treatment which is the remedy, for the trouble diagnosed. Why? It is partly due to the fact that the port manager is only a cog in the wheel, and is directed by the chairman and the two commissioners, resident in Ottawa, who know nothing about local conditions and who, from day to day, have not an opportunity to watch development, growth and needs of any and all the great ports of Canada.
For these reasons I am opposed to control by a board in Ottawa, unless its operations are confined to certain specific matters, one of which would be the control of capital expenditures by it through the Minister of Transport, and the placing of funds that come in through the port in the hands of the port manager in ordeT that they may be accounted for, used and expended under a central audit.
I have not had the honour of discussing this bill with the Minister of Marine, and so I cannot say just what are the government's intentions, but if this bill, in providing for central control at Ottawa, means that from this city there will go out to the various ports the supplies that are necessary for the operation, development and expansion of our harbour facilities, I say that this is not fair to the legitimate aspirations of the business people who are located at these ports. It will not give to our people in the various localities in which these great ports are located an opportunity to tender on a fair basis for the supplies that are necessary in connection with the operation of these ports. I may be judging too quickly, and if I am,

I owe an apology to the Minister of Marine. When the bill goes into committee, and we have an opportunity of analyzing acutely the various sections of the bill, I hope to hear from his lips just what is intended and what will be the effect of the legislation as it finally passes through this house to the upper chamber to become law and to govern our ports from one end of this country to the other.
There are many questions akin to that of harbour development. Many millions of dollars have been spent at the port of Halifax. The scheme of the port development there was first outlined under the Conservative war leader, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Laird Borden, who was advised by experts, and who contemplated the development of ocean terminals. The result to-day, I am sorry to say, is that at certain times, when gales or even strong winds are blowing from the southeast, some of the masters of the great ships feel that they have not the security that they would have if the inner harbour had been developed, as was projected by Mr. Kennedy, who laid out the harbour of Montreal. Later on, when under the Hon. Mr. Emmerson, Mr. Blair, and later under the late Hon. W.
S.	Fielding, as acting Minister of Railways, the port was developed, and what is known as the "Fielding pier," pier No. 2, was built, it was built as the first unit of the development of the inner harbour, a development that with McNab's island, Lawlor's island and George's island, made a great natural breakwater that God and nature placed there, and had that development been proceeded with conditions to-day would have been very much better. As Captain Webster of the Montclair said to me one day, "Mr. Finn, I feel safe enough to go to sleep if I can get my ship safely inside George's island with both anchors down, and then the wind, let her blow."
But the other scheme of development of the harbour was proceeded with. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, as he says, was present at the opening of the new pier, and I remember that he paid great compliments to the gentlemen who had occupied the position of chairman of the Halifax harbour board, one of whom retired through professional exigencies and the other by the will of the people. We should find to-day a bill introduced into this house to change the name of the Halifax harbour commission, due to appointments made by my right hon. friend and his colleagues. After the defeat of the provincial government led by Colonel Harrington, and prior to that by the Hon. Mr. Rhodes, ex-Minister of Finance, practically

National Harbours Board-Mr. Finn
every man that was guilty of attempting to steal the franchise from the people of Nova Scotia was dismissed after investigation. It became a political eleemosynary institution of the party of my right hon. friend opposite, and every one of those dismissed were tucked away into lovely positions which they still occupy, although very soon they will sleep on harder pillows. If efficiency is the great thing to be desired, then at least some hon. gentlemen opposite must cry out, "Mea culpa, mea culpa, mea maxima culpa."
I see another hon. gentleman opposite, for whom I have a great admiration, as I have for the right hon. leader of the opposition. I refer to the former Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), who reminded me only ten days or two weeks ago, as we walked out of the house together, that at an oratorical contest in Halifax, when I was attending Lasalle academy-he being one of the judges when I won the oratorical medal-said that he never dreamed that he would live to see us both sitting in this house at the same time. I am sure, however, that he always believed that if we should be in the house together we would be sitting on opposite sides and yet still be true personal friends.
My colleague from Halifax (Mr. Isnor), in speaking of this bill, has used the expression, "the long arm." Well, the long arm is sometimes used for one thing and sometimes for another. While I do not operate an automobile myself, they tell me that sometimes it is just as well to have both hands on the wheel; that you cannot operate a car with a long arm. I agree with my colleague in saying that the long arm, this distant treatment of our ports from Ottawa, is not the treatment that is calculated to bring about efficiency or that splendid expansion of our ports that we all look to see.
I regret that the debate on this bill could not be connected up with the debate on the bill to be introduced by the Minister of Railways and Canals in connection with the amendment of the Canadian National-Cana-dian Pacific Act. I was glad to hear that that act is to be scrapped. Why? I believe that the legislation creating that board of trustees was one of the greatest injustices ever done the Canadian National railway system. It was the beginning of the thin end of tire wedge to hand over gradually parts of the Canadian National system to Sir Edward Beatty and the gentlemen whom my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition characterized as the moneyed men of St. James street. The Canadian National railway system is one of which Canada might well be proud. If we
are saddled with the Canadian Northern railway; if we are saddled with the Grand Trunk railway, it is because those babies were placed on the doorstep of Liberalism. The credit of the country and the honour of our people have to stand behind them because they were taken over when Sir Robert Borden was Prime Minister of Canada to save some of the banks. He did not stop until he gave Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann ten millions of dollars for their equity of redemption when both these roads should have been sold under the hammer to the highest bidder. If that had been done the country would have been the richer.
I want to say before I sit down that I wish Sir Henry Thornton was alive to-day. I saw him in New York after he had retired from the presidency of the Canadian National system. I believe he was the biggest asset that the people of Canada ever had. It is true that he made vast expenditures, but he did this in the days when Canada was forging ahead and opportunity was knocking at our door, not for the last time or the first time. It was necessary to act, and he did so. He coordinated these great systems into one and kept them going until he stepped out of the presidency, I believe broken in heart and broken in body. It was said of the late President Wilson by Theodore Roosevelt, a former president of the United States, when he ran as leader of the bull moose party -he got what the bull got, a shot between the eyes, and then he went to Africa to shoot lions-that he wondered' when he crossed Shadow Lawn if he would not see the shadow of the Lusitania. He said, "Lusitania, Shadow Lawn, Woodrow Wilson enough for me." I often wonder whether there are not some people in Canada who are afraid that they may see the shadow of that great man, Sir Henry Thornton, who was so misunderstood and so maligned, yet so wonderful and so human.
A committee of parliament laid bare to the bone everything that he or his associates ever did. The right hon. leader of the opposition created the Duff commission to investigate the Canadian Pacific railway, but when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), sitting where my right hon. friend now sits, asked him whether this investigation would be made public, he replied that it would not. He was asked whether the report would be tabled and he said, "no." I do not want to misquote him, but he said that in his judgment it was not in the interests of the people and of Canada that the position of the Canadian Pacific railway should be known to the people of Canada.

I do not desire to be unfair to the leader of the opposition as I have too much respect for him, but the fact remains that everybody has not the right to go into the library and read that report. It was never distributed' in pamphlet form, as other matters of a public nature are distributed, so that the people of Canada might be conversant with a great public issue and be able to come to a conclusion in that regard. I well remember the words of the leader of the opposition when he said, "Competition ever, amalgamation never." In 1935 he changed his tune, as did a gentle^ man who crept into the Senate. This gentleman used to play a tin whistle so he was called "tinny." The right hon. gentleman said that if he was sent back to power he would have a plebiscite to ascertain whether the people of Canada wanted these great railway systems knit into one.
I say to-night, with all the sincerity, with all the force, vim and energy that I possess, that any hon. gentleman who has a responsibility such as the Prime Minister has, who would ask the young woman of twenty-one years of age or the young lad of twenty-one to decide whether or not millions upon millions of dollars of valuable assets including the very future of this country should be determined by them, though they know nothing about it, would be like taking a child out of the ABC class and asking him to prove a problem in geometry on the blackboard in the twelfth grade of one of the common schools of the country. No, Mr. Speaker. We must all remember our respon-

sibility. I am sure the leader of the opposition does, as does every hon. gentleman in this house. Sometimes we all speak hurriedly, quickly, in the heat of passion caused by sudden provocation, but I am sure that the leader of the opposition, while he has had great provocation at times to speak quickly, though always, I think, in a gentlemanly way, sometimes says things which he would prefer- as I have done myself, and I am not equal to him in stature or ability, but open confession is good for the soul-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
The principle underlying this bill involves such a departure from the system that has obtained heretofore that it cannot but be of great concern to members who sit for cities and towns which have harbour commissions, and particularly to those who sit for the city of Montreal.
Canada was, born on the banks of the St. Lawrence river, and its commercial growth was speeded up by the judicious use of our system of navigation, our river, which is a commerce carrier. The St. Lawrence river is the main artery that links up Canada with the rest of the world and its various provinces together. From Montreal, which is the head of ocean navigation in eastern Canada, our railway systems have radiated to all sections of our country. It is therefore of great concern to members sitting as I do for the city of Montreal that a system which has obtained heretofore and under which the harbour of Montreal has developed tremendously, as have those of so many other cities, should be radically changed.
I regret also that the time which has elapsed between the first reading of this bill and its second reading was not extended a little so that we might more thoroughly digest the various provisions embodied in the bill, which are of such great importance. Reference has often been made to the Gibb report on which the bill is mainly based. I have a great deal of respect for Sir Alexander Gibb and I should not like to speak disparagingly of his report, which in my opinion is of great value. Yet I think I should point out a few contradictions in the report, or at least a few contradictions between the facts therein recited and the conclusions arrived at by Sir Alexander Gibb.

National Harbours Board-Mr. Vien
In the first place, I would say, with due respect to Sir Alexander Gibb, that I do not regard him as infallible. He may very well make mistakes, and before acting upon his recommendations it might perhaps have been better to ponder over them a little longer. Be that as it may, I think there are more provisions than one in this bill which should be very carefully scrutinized. I have listened with a great deal of attention to the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and also by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). I very seldom agree with the leader of the opposition, but I must agree with him on some of the points he has raised, very forcibly I think, in the remarks which he has made on this subject.
In the first place, even a board created directly under the supervision of the minister of the Department of Railways or of the Department of Marine will not be infallible, and it may make numerous mistakes which may be just as great, if not greater, than those that have been pointed out in some instances of the administration of our Canadian harbours. I am inclined to believe that people who reside in a particular locality are better able to judge the requirements of that locality and properly to administer the properties of the harbour and to develop the facilities therein involved than are people, who would be rather bureaucratic, in one of the departments of the state.
In the second place I would point out that conditions which will prevail at Vancouver may be very different from those at Halifax or Saint John, and that the conditions and requirements of the St. Lawrence river and of the ports of Montreal, Three Rivers or Quebec may be very different from those of other sections of our country. I should be inclined to trust the good judgment of those residing in the locality, fully cognizant of its requirements and needs, rather than the judgment of certain gentlemen for whom I have a great deal of respect but who may not have the same knowledge of local problems and local requirements. I am in favour of modifying to some extent the system which has prevailed heretofore. It has been rightly said that some expenditures were not warranted; but it seems to me that this state of affairs could have been rectified without the necessity of going the full length of the provisions of this bill. It could be provided without much legislation, that all capital expenditures should be carefully scrutinized and submitted to the formalities of a vote in parliament or of an order in council. Legislation much more simple than this bill might
also provide for the proper auditing of the accounts and the operating expenditures of the harbours of Canada. This could very easily be introduced in our legislation, without all the clauses and dispositions of this bill.
I should like to point out that Sir Alexander Gibb in his report pays a high tribute to the harbour of Montreal in which I am directly interested. At page 15 of his report he says:
There is strong evidence that the commissions of Montreal and Vancouver played an important part in this progress. They provided a type of administration at least the equal of any that was to be found elsewhere on the North American continent; and notwithstanding mistakes, which no system can prevent, the developments under the two harbour commissions have generally been sound and economically justified.
That conclusion, based upon his investigation of the facts, would seem to militate for the continuance of a system which so far has proved to be efficient. And then he begins to consider what has been done elsewhere. There will be found, at pages 29 and 30, an analysis of the systems in other countries, and he points out at page .28 of his report how after coming to a centralization of administration of the ports, they have now reverted to a greater autonomy being given to various harbours; and I have a study of the various acts which have been of late put upon the statute books of the French Republic. On January 5, 1912, a law was enacted giving back to several harbours in France local autonomy, and this local autonomy or authority was further enlarged by the law of June 12, 1920. Under these laws local authorities get corporate entities and full autonomy with respect to the administration of the harbours.

speechtext: What harbours were those? Could the hon. gentleman give us the names? Cherbourg? Le Havre?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Particularly Bordeaux and
Le Havre. But the law is not limited to those harbours at all, and local authorities can be constituted under the law for the management of harbours other than those that I have just mentioned. Therefore, if this system of centralization was tried in France and was found less efficient than the local autonomy, I would be a little diffident about introducing this system in Canada without more careful study and investigation.
Sir Alexander Gibb compares the harbour of Montreal with those of other countries. I find at page 71 of his report some very inter-

esting comparisons. At paragraph 148 Sir Alexander Gibb speaks of the operating costs in the harbour of Montreal, and says this:
Operating costs judged by ordinary standards do not at first sight appear excessive, for a port that is open for barely two-thirds of the year. But in the first place maintenance and repairs are not being wholly carried by the operating costs as they should be, and secondly on looking more closely into the accounts, there are obvious opportunities for reduction of costs without impairing efficiency. For instance the salaries and expenses of the administrative staff and offices account for 20 per cent of the total operating expenditure, and this is excessive; again the harbour railway shows a loss which should be avoidable. In the table below I have divided the costs over the principal departments, each carrying its proportionate share of the administration.
But though he shows there some room for improvement, he continues, by giving a comparison of the tolls collected at Montreal and the rates under which they are collected with those of various ports in the world, and he says:
Montreal thus compares very favourably with the average secured by large ocean ports elsewhere, particularly if allowance be made for the short season. On the basis of the present cost of constructing a first-class berth with sheds and full equipment in Montreal harbour, and assuming the present scale of charges and costs, the traffic required to cover operating expenditure, interest and replacement, would be about 240,000 tons of general cargo and grain per berth per year. The average annual figure is now about 135,000 tons, but in the peak year it rose to 165,000 tons per berth. It would from this appear that an ocean berth at Montreal can only be made self-supporting by raising port charges

a method which cannot be advocated; or by improving the handling capacity and the turn around of vessels, on the importance of which I have already laid stress.
The figure for gross receipts per ton handled, namely 47 cents, appears moderate, and that this is so is borne out by the results of my investigations into the cost of the port of Montreal from the shipping and user's points of view, as compared with other Canadian and United States ports. I have set out in table XIX the average normal costs of a tramp loading bulk grain, and a liner handling general cargo in Montreal, assuming no exceptional delays.
According to my information, and from the careful inquiries that I have made, I am satisfied that these costs are not seriously challenged by competing ports, except where the latter may be partially assisted by special rail rates, (p. 73.)
Therefore, it seems to me that this report is not a severe criticism of the present state of affairs in Montreal. There is no condition revealed at 'that point that would absolutely justify a departure from the system now in existence. As I have just mentioned, it seems to me that it would be rather a step

backward to cause the local districts to lose their autonomy and to suggest that a board created under the present legislation and centralized in any department of the government should be more efficient in managing the affairs of all the harbours of Canada. The management of the affairs of a big harbour is a big work, and if it has been necessary hitherto to maintain commissions in Halifax, Saint John, Quebec, Montreal, to say nothing of Vancouver, Toronto and New Westminster, surely it would be rather hazardous to centralize in the hands of only three men sitting in Ottawa the management of all our harbours.
As I have said, I should like to see some amendment to the present legislation to make it abundantly clear that no capital expenditure will be permitted until it is first voted by parliament and then authorized by order in council, and that such expenditures, either capital or operating, should be properly audited and placed' under the jurisdiction of the auditor general of Canada.

I agree with the right hon. gentleman, who mentioned this previously. To my mind that would be a constructive amendment to the present system, and there is nothing to prevent the minister charged with the administration of the various harbour commissions from having a closer control over them. It is with a great deal of misgiving, however, that I view this change from a system which Sir Alexander Gibb was obliged to admit had given admirable results hitherto, in order to try something which had been experimented with in other countries and which in at least some instances, such as the harbours of Le Havre and Bordeaux, had to be given up. In the United States there is no central control over the big harbours. It may be said, as Sir Alexander Gibb points out, that in some harbours such as New York and others there has been overdevelopment, ahead of the requirements of trade and commerce. It seems to me, however, that this system has been of great assistance in the development of our harbour facilities so essential to our trade and commerce.
If I might be permitted to do so, Mr. Speaker, I would ask that you now call it eleven o'clock, and I would move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
